Bigeye grenadier (Macrourus holotrachys) exhibits life-history traits characteristic of deep-dwelling, slow-growing teleosts found on continental slopes and abyssal plains. The species attains a considerable adult body size, with maximum recorded individuals reaching an ultimate total length of 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], a value derived from pre-anal length measurements converted using established morphometric relationships. Neonates, by contrast, emerge from pelagic eggs at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.001 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.001 grams], a mass consistent with the minute, yolk-dependent yolk-sac larvae typical of macrourid fishes. This initial body mass is calculated from an egg diameter of approximately 1.3 millimeters, reflecting the limited maternal investment per offspring that characterizes a highly fecund, broadcast-spawning reproductive strategy. The pronounced disparity between neonatal and adult mass underscores the extended growth trajectory and substantial somatic investment required before individuals approach asymptotic size.

At the onset of sexual maturation, individuals of Macrourus holotrachys reach a total length at puberty of 61.6 centimeters [Lp = 61.6 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to a pre-anal length of roughly 21 centimeters after conversion using the same morphometric factor employed for ultimate length. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 1000 grams [Wwp = approximately 1000 grams], a body mass derived from a length–weight relationship (W = aL^b) fitted to regional specimen data. This mass at maturation represents a substantial fraction of the ultimate body size and suggests that reproductive activity is deferred until a considerable proportion of lifetime somatic growth has been completed. The energetic investment required to reach this size in the cold, food-limited environment of the deep sea likely imposes strong selective pressures on the timing of first spawning.

In terms of maximum reproductive potential, laboratory and field observations conducted at a stable water temperature of 2.5°C [T = 2.5°C] indicate that gravid females can produce up to approximately 712 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 712 eggs per spawning event] during the peak of the spawning period. This high fecundity per event, combined with a protracted spawning season that may last several months, allows individuals to achieve a substantial annual reproductive output despite the slow pace of life in abyssal environments. The elevated rate at such a low temperature is notable, as metabolic processes in ectothermic deep-sea fishes are generally constrained by the cold; the observed values suggest that Macrourus holotrachys has evolved a particularly efficient reproductive physiology for its thermal regime.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults of Bigeye grenadier reaches approximately 4900 grams [Wwi = approximately 4900 grams], a body mass corresponding to the length–weight relationship applied to the maximum total length of 100 centimeters. This value situates Macrourus holotrachys among the larger members of its genus, placing it well above the typical asymptotic mass of many congeners such as Macrourus berglax, and reflects the combined effects of extended longevity and slow but sustained somatic growth in a thermally stable but resource-poor habitat. Comparative data from related macrourid species suggest that ultimate body mass is a strong predictor of both age at maturity and lifetime fecundity in this clade, reinforcing the role of size as a key life-history axis.

The maximum lifespan of Macrourus holotrachys has been estimated at 9125 days [am = 9125 days] based on otolith increment analysis of specimens collected from the Southern Ocean and adjacent waters, with these longevity estimates made at an ambient temperature of 4.5°C [T = 4.5°C]. This translates to a lifespan of approximately 25 years, placing the species among the longer-lived grenadiers and consistent with the extended generation times typical of deep-sea demersal fishes. Such longevity, combined with the deferred maturation and moderate fecundity, implies a relatively low intrinsic rate of population increase, making the species potentially vulnerable to overexploitation where it is caught as bycatch in deepwater trawl fisheries.
